transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... my wife is the one who really pushed me to come talk to somebody. What brings me in is that I just can't get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. I mean, the cracks, the sun spots, the sagging... it's all I can focus on. 

Like, whenever I have to go into town and sit down with the banker or the county extension people, I just know they're staring right at my skin. I was actually just at the bank last Tuesday talking about a loan for some new irrigation equipment. The prices on aluminum pipe these days, I swear, they must think we're growing gold out there in the dirt. And don't even get me started on fertilizer costs this season. It’s enough to make you want to just sell the whole plot to developers like the Miller brothers did down the road. They put up a whole subdivision of identical houses right on top of some of the best prime topsoil in the county, which is just a crying shame if you ask me... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the bank. Sitting across from those folks in their clean suits, I just feel like they're zeroing in on every crack and spot on my face and hands. My wife tells me I'm making it up. She says I just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. But I just can't get past it.
Are you worried about how you look in other ways, besides your face and hands?

No, not really. It's just the skin. I mean, I've got a bit of a gut, but what guy my age doesn't? Specially when my wife makes those casseroles of hers. She's got this one with the tater tots on top—maybe you've had something like it? It's a real rib-sticker. We had it just the other night after I spent all day trying to fix the old John Deere. The starter motor on that thing is just about shot, and getting parts for a model that old is like pulling teeth. I was on the phone with three different suppliers in three different states, and nobody has the right armature. It's ridiculous how they just stop making parts for good, reliable machines and expect you to drop a hundred grand on a new one with all these computers in it. A tractor doesn't need a computer, it needs a good engine and a strong PTO. You know what I mean? 

But, uh, no. Just my face and my hands. They just look... ruined.
Do you find yourself thinking about the appearance of your face and hands at times when you're not looking in a mirror or interacting with others?

Well, yeah, I suppose I do think about it when I'm just out working. Like yesterday, I was out mending the fence line down by the south pasture. The deer keep pushing through and snapping the wire. You'd think they'd just go around, but no, they gotta barrel right through the weakest spot. I was out there with the pliers, pulling the wire tight, and I just kept staring at my hands. The knuckles are so thick, and the skin is just... leathery. 

It got me thinking about how much work those hands have done, sure, but also how they just look so awful now. And then I missed the staple and hit my thumb with the hammer. Hurt like the dickens. Had to go inside and run it under the cold water. My wife, she just shook her head at me. She was in the middle of making some of that sweet tea she does, the kind where she boils the sugar right into the water before adding the tea bags. It's the only way to do it, really. If you just stir sugar into cold tea, it just sits at the bottom of the glass like sand. You gotta make a syrup first. 

But yeah, I guess I do think about it even when I'm by myself. It's just hard not to, you know? They're right there in front of me all the time.
Has worrying about the appearance of your face and hands ever caused you to avoid social or work-related activities?

Well, yeah, it has. I mean, I've actually missed calls with the bankers and put off making some pretty important farm decisions because I just... I couldn't get myself looking acceptable enough to go sit down with those people. You know, you try to wash up, scrub the dirt out, but the cracks are still there. It's like trying to polish a cinderblock. 

And my wife, she runs this little craft thing and hosts these retreats out at the farm. She's always wanting to take pictures for the website or whatever to promote it. I used to do it, but I've stopped agreeing to be in any of those photos. I don't want my face plastered all over the internet for everyone to see. Speaking of the internet, though, it's a real mess out our way. We're supposed to have that high-speed fiber optic whatever, but they stopped laying the cable about two miles down the county road. Just stopped! Said they ran out of funding or hit some rock shelf they didn't expect. So we're stuck with this satellite dish that cuts out every time a decent cloud rolls over. You can't even check the radar to see if rain's coming because the rain blocks the signal! It's completely backwards. The guy who came out to install it was this young kid, couldn't have been more than twenty, and he backed his van right over my wife's prize hostas. Just flattened 'em. She was furious. 

But, uh, yeah. I don't go to town as much, and I definitely don't let her take my picture anymore. It's just easier that way.
Do you think your face and hands are the only things that are flawed about your appearance, or are there other parts of your body that you worry about as well?

No, no, like I said before, it's really just the face and the hands. I mean, sure, I'm not as spry as I used to be, but that's just getting older. My knees pop like bubble wrap when I stand up, but everybody's do at my age. You should hear my buddy Earl when he gets out of his truck. Sounds like a bowl of Rice Krispies. He drives this old Ford F-250, must be a '98 or '99, with the 7.3 liter diesel. Now that was a real engine. They don't make them like that anymore. You could run that thing on cooking oil if you had to. Earl actually tried that once, strained a bunch of grease from the diner in town. Smelled like french fries driving down the highway. Made everybody behind him hungry, I bet. But then he didn't filter it right one time and clogged the fuel injectors. Cost him a pretty penny to get that fixed. The mechanic in town, old man Henderson, he gave Earl an earful about it. Henderson's been fixing trucks since before I was born, I think. He's got this shop that looks like a strong breeze would knock it over, but he knows his stuff. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right. No, it's just the skin on my face and hands that bothers me. Everything else is just regular wear and tear, I guess.
Have your concerns about the appearance of your face and hands changed at all over time, or have they stayed pretty much the same?

Well, I don't know if they've changed, really. I guess I haven't kept track of it like that. It feels like it's just always been this way, you know? Like how the weather patterns have been shifting. Used to be you could set your watch by the spring rains, but now? Now it's dry as a bone until June, and then it all comes down at once and washes the topsoil right into the creek. 

Speaking of the creek, the beavers have moved back in down past the old oak tree. Dammed up the whole thing. The water backed up into the lower pasture and made a real mess of things. I had to get the tractor down there and try to pull some of the brush out just to get it flowing again. That tractor, let me tell you, it's a John Deere, one of the older models, a 4020. Best machine they ever built. My dad bought it brand new back in '68. We've rebuilt the engine twice, but it still runs like a top. The new ones, they've got all these computers and sensors. If a wire gets loose, the whole thing shuts down and you gotta call a technician out with a laptop just to tell you what's wrong. A laptop! To fix a tractor! It's ridiculous. Give me a wrench and a grease gun any day. 

But, uh, yeah. I don't think my worries about my face and hands have changed much. Just seems like they've always been awful.
Do you think people are actually judging you because of the way your face and hands look, or is it more that you just wish they looked different?

Well, I definitely think they're judging me. I mean, that's what brought me in here to begin with. I just can't get past how rough and worn out my face and hands look. When I'm sitting across from the bankers or the county extension folks, I know they're staring right at the cracks and the sun spots and all the sagging skin. My wife, she tries to be nice about it, says I just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. 

But she doesn't get it. She's got that nice, soft skin. She uses this lotion she buys from a catalog, smells like lavender. Lavender's a funny plant, you know. We tried growing some out near the side garden a few years back to keep the deer away. Supposedly, deer hate the smell of it. But I'll tell you what, the deer around our place must have no sense of smell because they marched right through that lavender and ate every single one of my wife's prize tomatoes. Just took one bite out of each one and left the rest to rot on the vine. It's infuriating. The deer population has just exploded lately. Used to be you'd see a buck during hunting season and that was it, but now they're practically knocking on the back door asking for a handout. My neighbor, Jim, he put up an eight-foot fence around his whole property to keep them out. Cost him a fortune. He used that heavy-gauge wire, the kind they use for cattle. 

But yeah, anyway, the bankers... they're definitely staring. I can feel it. I know they think I look terrible.

When you think people are staring at your face and hands, is it because you believe they're seeing something inherently wrong with them, or is it because you're afraid of what they might think of you as a person?

Well, I guess it's... it's because there *is* something wrong with them. I mean, like I was saying, that's what brings me in. I just can't get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. When I'm sitting there, I know every banker or county person is staring right at the cracks and the spots and all the sagging skin. It's just awful. My wife, she tries to say I just look like a man who's worked outdoors, but... she doesn't see what I see. 

And speaking of working outdoors, the county folks, they've been coming around a lot more lately. They're talking about widening the county road that runs past the north edge of our property. Claim they need more clearance for the big logging trucks coming down from the ridge. Those logging trucks, I tell you, they come barreling down that hill like they've lost their brakes. And the dust they kick up! It settles on everything. I had to wash the siding on the house twice last summer just to see the paint. Used a pressure washer I borrowed from Jim. It's a gas-powered one, Honda engine. Starts on the first pull every time. I've been meaning to buy one myself, but you know how it is, always something else needs fixing first. Like the roof on the old barn, lost some shingles in that windstorm back in October. 

But, uh, anyway. Yeah. It's because they look so bad. The cracks and the spots. That's what they're staring at, I just know it.
When you think about how your face and hands look, is it the appearance itself that bothers you or what other people might think of you because of it?

Well, I guess... I guess I'm not entirely sure which it is. I mean, it's the appearance that bothers me, sure, but I don't really know if it's just that or what folks are thinking. I haven't really sat down and tried to pick apart the difference, you know? It just all feels bad. 

Speaking of picking things apart, I had to completely dismantle the carburetor on that 4020 last week. The float was sticking, flooding the whole engine. You wouldn't believe the gunk that builds up in there over the years. Modern gas, it just doesn't sit well. It breaks down, turns to varnish if you leave it in the tank over the winter. I started using this fuel stabilizer, comes in a little red bottle. Supposed to keep it fresh for up to two years. Two years! I don't know if I believe that. My uncle Bob, he used to swear by putting a little bit of diesel in with his gas to keep things lubricated, but I wouldn't try that on a newer engine. Bob was a character, though. He used to witch for water. You know, with the willow branches? Swore he could find a well on any piece of land. And you know, he found the spot for our main well back in '75. Hasn't run dry once, even in the drought of '88. 

But, uh, yeah. I don't really know if it's the look of my hands and face or what people think about them. I just know I hate how they look.
Do you think you would still be bothered by the appearance of your face and hands if you lived in complete isolation with no contact with other people?

Well, I... I don't really know. I've never really thought about living completely alone like that. I mean, I suppose if nobody was around to see me, maybe it wouldn't be as bad? But I just don't know for sure. 

Honestly, the idea of living in complete isolation sounds a lot like my cousin Earl's setup. Earl moved up to the panhandle back in the late nineties, bought himself a hundred acres of nothing but scrub brush and rocks. Built a cabin out of old shipping containers. He's completely off the grid. Solar panels, rainwater catchment, the whole nine yards. He even rigged up a system to run his old Ford Ranger on used cooking oil he gets from a diner two towns over. Smells like french fries every time he drives by. It's the darnedest thing. But Earl, he's always been a bit of a hermit. Even when we were kids, he'd rather be out in the woods trapping raccoons than playing baseball with the rest of us. He used to tan the hides himself. Stretched them out on these wooden hoops he made from hickory saplings. Hickory is a tough wood, you know. Hard on the tools. You try to cut hickory with a dull blade and you'll just end up smoking the wood and burning out your saw motor. I learned that the hard way when I was clearing out the old fencerow down by the creek. 

But, uh, anyway... living alone? I don't know. I'm just not sure if it would change how much I hate looking at my own hands and face. I just don't know.
Would you still feel the need to improve the appearance of your face and hands if you were certain that nobody else was judging you?

Well, I... I honestly couldn't tell you. If I knew for an absolute fact nobody was judging me? I don't know if I'd still be trying to fix them. Maybe? It's just hard to picture. 

People are always judging something, though, aren't they? It's just human nature. Kind of like the livestock judging at the county fair. Last year, my neighbor Tom entered his prize Hereford steer. Beautiful animal, really blocky and well-muscled. But the judge, some young guy they brought down from the State University, he docked Tom points because he said the steer's stance in the hindquarters was a fraction too wide. A fraction of an inch! Tom was just furious. He’d spent six months getting the feed ratio on that animal just right. He uses this custom mix of cracked corn, oats, and sweet molasses. 

That molasses, I'll tell you, it gets absolutely everywhere if you aren't careful. You get a drop of it on your work boots, and the barn cats will follow you around the yard all afternoon trying to lick it off the leather. We had this one barn cat, a little mouser we called Barnaby—well, we called him Barnaby right up until she went and had a litter of five kittens right on the seat of my combine tractor. Left a terrible mess on the upholstery. I had to scrub it with a wire brush and baking soda just to get the smell out before harvest. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Right, about not being judged. I just... I really don't know. I can't say for sure if I'd still feel the need to improve my skin or not. It's just too hard to imagine a situation like that.
If you were completely confident that nobody would reject or judge you because of your face and hands, would you still want to change their appearance?

I... I really don't know. If I was completely confident nobody would judge me? I just don't know if I'd still want to change them. It's like asking if the sun would still rise if the rooster didn't crow. I just can't say for sure. 

Speaking of roosters, we had this Rhode Island Red when I was a boy. Meanest bird you ever laid eyes on. Used to chase my sister all the way from the chicken coop to the back porch. He had these huge spurs, sharp as a pocket knife. My dad finally had enough of it and decided that rooster was going in the stew pot. Plucking a chicken is a terrible job, you know. The smell of the wet feathers, it just sticks in your nose. We used to dip them in scalding water first to loosen the quills. You have to get the temperature just right, around 145 degrees, or you'll cook the skin and it tears when you pull the feathers. My grandmother had this huge cast-iron kettle she used just for scalding chickens. Must have weighed fifty pounds empty. Cast iron is great, though. Holds the heat forever. I still use her old skillet to fry up potatoes in the morning. Best way to get them crispy on the edges. You fry 'em in a little bit of bacon grease, maybe throw in some diced onions...

But, um, anyway. If nobody judged me? I just... I don't have an answer for that. I really don't know if I'd still want to change how my face and hands look.
Is it the actual look of your face and hands that bothers you, or is it more about how you think others might react to them?

Well, I... I really couldn't tell you. Is it just the look of them, or is it other people reacting? I don't know how to pull those two things apart, to be honest. I just don't know. 

It kind of reminds me of how folks react to my old John Deere tractor. The green paint is all peeled off the hood, and the fenders are rusted clear through in spots. People drive by and probably think it's just a piece of junk ready for the scrap heap. But she runs like an absolute top. I rebuilt the carburetor myself last spring. Carburetors can be real finicky, you know, if you don't know exactly what you're doing. If you don't get the float adjusted just right, you'll flood the engine before you even turn the key. My buddy Dale did that out in his south pasture a few years back. Flooded his rig so bad he had to walk three miles back to his house in the mud. And the mud out by his place, it's that thick, red clay. It sticks to your boots until they weigh ten pounds a piece. You have to take a hose and a putty knife just to get the treads clean before you can even walk up the porch steps. His wife, Mary, she wouldn't let him in the house for an hour. Made him strip down to his long johns right there in the front yard. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my face and hands. Yeah, I just... I really don't know if it's the actual look of them that bothers me or what people think. I just can't say for sure.
Is it possible that you would feel okay about the appearance of your face and hands if you were completely alone and had no interactions with other people?

Well, I... I honestly couldn't tell you. If I was completely alone, like a hermit or something? I just don't know if I'd feel okay about them or not. It's really hard to say. 

Being completely alone, though... that brings me back to the winter of '98. I spent three weeks straight up at the old hunting cabin, completely cut off from the world. The snow was so deep you couldn't get a truck up the ridge if you tried. I had to snowshoe in just to check on the roof. Snowshoes are tricky if you aren't used to them. You have to walk with this wide-legged gait, almost like a duck, or you'll cross the frames and trip yourself right into a snowbank. I had these traditional ash-wood ones with the rawhide lacing. You have to varnish them every couple of seasons or the moisture rots the gut right out of them. Varnish is getting so expensive these days, too. I went down to the hardware store in town last week, and a quart of marine spar varnish was nearly thirty dollars. Can you believe that? And the kid working the counter didn't even know what I was asking for when I said spar varnish. He had to go get the manager. The manager, Bill, he and I actually played high school football together. He was a defensive tackle, big guy, but he blew out his knee senior year right before the playoffs. Never quite walked the same after that. 

But, um, wait, what was the question? Oh, about being alone and my skin. Yeah, I just... I really don't know if being isolated would make me feel any better about my face and hands. I just can't picture it making a difference, but I really don't know.
Would you say that your main concern is what other people think of your face and hands, or is it more about how you personally feel when you look at them?

Well, I... I just don't know. Is it what other people think, or how I feel when I look at them? I couldn't rightly say which one is the main thing. It's just a big jumble in my head, to be honest. I don't know.

Looking at things, though... it's like when I try to look at the back forty from the kitchen window. The glass in that old window is original to the house, you know. It's that wavy, antique glass with the little bubbles trapped inside it. My wife, God rest her soul, always wanted me to replace it with those modern double-pane vinyl things. Said it let a draft in during the winter. But I always loved how the light caught those little imperfections in the glass right around sunset. Sunset out here is something else, especially in the late fall when the corn is all harvested and the dust is still settling. The sky turns this incredible shade of bruised purple and bright orange. We used to sit out on the porch with a glass of iced tea and just watch it. Sweet tea, of course. You have to boil the water first, steep the bags for exactly five minutes, and stir the sugar in while it's still piping hot so it dissolves right. If you try to put sugar in cold tea, it just sinks to the bottom like sand in a riverbed. You'll be drinking plain tea until the last sip, and then it's like drinking syrup. I hate that. 

But, uh... I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. What were we talking about? Oh, my face and hands and what bothers me most. Yeah, I just... I really can't tell you if it's my own feelings or other people's thoughts that are the main concern. I just don't know.
When you think about your face and hands, is it your own dissatisfaction with how they look that bothers you the most?

Well, I... I just can't say for sure. Is it my own dissatisfaction? I don't know. Every time I try to pin it down, it just slips away from me. I really don't know what bothers me the most about them.

Dissatisfaction, though... that's a funny word. It makes me think of the time I bought that new brand of feed for the hogs back in '05. The salesman swore up and down it had a better protein mix, said it would put weight on them twice as fast as the old stuff. I bought a whole pallet of it, stacked right up to the rafters in the barn. But those hogs, they wouldn't even touch it. They'd just sniff at the trough and look up at me like I'd insulted their mothers. Hogs are a lot smarter than people give them credit for, you know. They can recognize faces and they remember things for years. My granddad had a sow named Bessie who figured out how to unlatch the gate to the vegetable garden. She'd wait until everyone was asleep, sneak in, and eat all the prize-winning tomatoes, leaving the green ones alone. Granddad tried putting a padlock on it, but he lost the key in the tall grass out by the silo. We spent three days looking for that key with a metal detector. You ever use one of those? They make this high-pitched whining noise that just burrows right into your brain. I had a headache for a week after that. 

But, um... sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, about my face and hands and if it's my own dissatisfaction. Yeah, I just... I really couldn't tell you if that's the main thing. I just don't know.
Is it more that you dislike how your face and hands look to yourself, or that you think others might be judging you because of their appearance?

I mean, I really couldn't tell you. Is it me disliking them, or worrying about folks judging me? I just... I don't know. It's hard to pull those two things apart in my mind. 

Judging, though... boy, that reminds me of the county fair back in, oh, must have been '89. We were showing our Charolais cattle. The judge that year was old man Higgins. He took judging so seriously, walked around the ring with this clipboard and a bolo tie that had a piece of turquoise on it the size of a plum. I always wondered where he got that tie. Turquoise mostly comes from out West, you know, like New Mexico or Nevada. My younger brother took a trip out to Nevada once, drove his camper all the way across the country. Said he wanted to see the Hoover Dam. Did you know the concrete in the Hoover Dam is still curing? It's so thick that the chemical reaction is still generating heat inside, even after all these years. If they had poured it all at once, it would have taken a hundred and twenty-five years to cool down, so they had to pour it in these interlocking blocks. Engineering like that just fascinates me. They had to run pipes with ice water through the concrete just to keep it from cracking apart. 

But, uh... gosh, I'm sorry. I wandered off again, didn't I? What was it you were asking me? Oh, right, about whether it's me or other people judging my face and hands. Yeah, I just... I honestly don't know the answer to that. I couldn't say which one it is.
Is it the thought of others seeing your face and hands that bothers you, or is it more about how you feel when you look at them yourself?

I just... I honestly can't figure it out. Whether it's me looking or them looking... I don't know. It's like trying to untangle a knot, I guess. 

Untangling knots... well, that makes me think of the old baling twine we used to use. The old sisal twine, you know? It had that distinct smell, kind of earthy and dusty, and it was always getting tangled up if you didn't pull it from the center of the spool just right. We'd stack square bales in the loft for days in the summer heat. You'd get so sweaty the chaff would stick to your arms and neck like glue. We had this barn cat back then, a real mean-looking tabby with half an ear missing, who used to sleep right on top of the highest bales. He was a fantastic mouser, though. I once saw him catch a field mouse mid-air. Mice are a real problem out in the outbuildings if you don't keep ahead of them. They'll chew through absolutely anything. They even chewed right through the wiring harness on my old F-150 a few winters back. Cost me a fortune to get it towed and rewired, because you can't just splice those modern wires together easily anymore. They have all these specific voltage requirements for the computer sensors, and if you get it wrong, the whole dashboard lights up like a Christmas tree...

But, oh, shoot. I'm talking your ear off about mice and trucks now, aren't I? I'm sorry, my mind just wanders off. You asked about... about my face and hands, right? And whose thoughts bother me more. Honestly, doc, I just don't have a clear answer for you. It's all just one big heavy feeling, and I really can't tell where it starts or who it's about.
Is it more that you are upset by your own view of your face and hands, or that you believe others are judging you because of how they look?

I swear, Doc, you keep asking it, and I keep trying to dig deep and figure it out, but I just... I don't know. My own view, their view... it's all just a jumble in my head. 

View, though... you know, the best view I ever had was from the cab of this old International Harvester combine I used to run back in the late 90s. We were cutting winter wheat up near the county line. The dust would kick up so bad in the late afternoon, but when the sun hit it just right, it looked like the whole field was made of solid gold. I loved that old machine, even though the air conditioning never worked right. You had to keep the door propped open with a block of wood just to get a breeze. My buddy Earl, he tried to fix the AC once. Earl was an absolute wizard with a wrench, could fix anything with an engine. He actually built a go-kart out of a riding mower and an old washing machine motor for his grandkids. Those kids would tear up and down the gravel driveway until the sun went down. Gravel's tough to maintain, though. You get one good heavy spring rainstorm and it washes half your driveway right into the drainage ditch. Then you gotta pay someone to come out with a grader and smooth it all back out, and diesel fuel ain't cheap these days...

Wait, what was I... oh, for heaven's sake. I did it again, didn't I? I'm sorry. You're asking about my face and hands, and if it's me being upset or other people judging. Look, I really wish I could give you a straight answer, but I just don't have one. I just can't tell which one it is.
Is it more that you dislike your face and hands when you look at them, or that you worry about what others think when they see them?

I really, honestly don't know. I feel like a broken record here, Doc, but I just can't say if it's me hating the sight of them or me worrying about everyone else. It just all blends together. 

Blending together... that's exactly what happened when my wife tried to make her own tomato juice one year. We had this bumper crop of Roma tomatoes, just bushels of them. She got out this old heavy-duty blender her mother gave her for a wedding present back in '82. That thing was built like a tank, weighed about twenty pounds, with this thick glass pitcher. Anyway, she was blending batch after batch, and she decided to throw in some jalapeños from the garden to give it a kick. Well, she didn't realize how hot those peppers were that year. We had a really dry August, and dry weather makes peppers spicier, you know. Something about the capsaicin concentrating when the plant is stressed for water. It's the same reason why dry-farmed wine grapes supposedly make better wine, because the roots have to dig so deep into the soil to find moisture, bringing up all those minerals. A fella I met at the feed store once told me he tried growing grapes on his property, but the deer kept eating the shoots before they could even establish a vine. Deer are a real nuisance. They'll jump a six-foot fence like it's nothing if they see something they want to eat on the other side...

Oh, for crying out loud. I'm sorry, Doc. I did it again. I just start talking and my brain just takes a left turn. You were asking about my face and hands again, right? Yeah, I just... I wish I could give you a better answer, but I just don't know which one bothers me more.

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance

patient.answer:
Well, I guess... my wife is the one who really pushed me to come talk to somebody. What brings me in is that I just can't get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. I mean, the cracks, the sun spots, the sagging... it's all I can focus on. 

Like, whenever I have to go into town and sit down with the banker or the county extension people, I just know they're staring right at my skin.
